title: SQL Day 2 — DISTINCT, Sorting & Aggregated Business Views
description: Move from retrieving records into producing unique, ordered, top-N, grouped, and thresholded business results.

teaching.teacher:
## DISTINCT
DISTINCT removes duplicate combinations from the selected output. Use it when the business question asks for unique categories, regions, or customers.
teaching.explain: SELECT DISTINCT category FROM orders; returns each category once.
teaching.detailedlearning: DISTINCT applies to the entire selected combination. DISTINCT category, region means unique category-region pairs.
teaching.expose: When a manager says 'list each unique...' think DISTINCT.
teaching.business_question: The regional sales manager wants a list of every unique product category represented in the transaction table.

questions.scenario: The manager is preparing a category review.
Leadership wants to understand the regions represented in the order book.
The analyst is building a customer coverage check.
questions.request: Return each unique customer name once.
questions.validation: Each customer appears at most once.

topics.title: ORDER BY
topics.business_skill: Sort analytical results for ranking and review.

teaching.teacher:
## ORDER BY
ORDER BY controls result ordering. ASC is ascending; DESC is descending.
teaching.explain: ORDER BY sales DESC places the highest sales first.
teaching.detailedlearning: Sorting is essential for rankings and management review. Add a deterministic secondary sort when ties matter.
teaching.expose: Words like highest, lowest, largest, smallest, latest, and earliest are signals for ORDER BY.
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, sales FROM orders ORDER BY sales DESC;
teaching.business_question: The sales manager wants orders listed from the highest sales value to the lowest.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, customer_name, sales FROM orders ORDER BY sales DESC;

questions.scenario: The manager wants the largest transactions first.
questions.request: Return order ID and sales sorted from highest to lowest sales.

questions.scenario: Finance is reviewing the most profitable transactions first.
questions.request: Return order ID, customer name, and profit sorted from highest to lowest profit.

questions.scenario: Operations wants the largest quantities reviewed first.
questions.request: Return order ID, product name, and quantity sorted from highest to lowest quantity, then order ID ascending for ties.
questions.validation: Quantity DESC with order_id ASC tie-break.

teaching.teacher:
## LIMIT
LIMIT restricts the number of rows returned. Combined with ORDER BY it creates a Top-N analysis.
teaching.explain: ORDER BY sales DESC LIMIT 5 returns the five highest-sales orders.
teaching.detailedlearning: LIMIT without ORDER BY is not a business ranking. Always sort first when the requirement says top or bottom.
teaching.expose: 'Top 5', 'first 10', and 'highest 20' require a ranking rule before LIMIT.
teaching.example: SELECT order_id, sales FROM orders ORDER BY sales DESC LIMIT 5;
teaching.business_question: The commercial director wants the five largest individual orders by sales.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT order_id, customer_name, sales FROM orders ORDER BY sales DESC LIMIT 5;

questions.scenario: The manager needs a quick list of the three largest orders.
questions.request: Return the top three orders by sales.
questions.validation: Exactly three rows, highest sales first.

questions.scenario: Finance wants the five orders with the highest profit.
questions.request: Return the top five orders by profit.
questions.validation: Exactly five rows, highest profit first.

questions.scenario: Operations is investigating the largest unit orders.
questions.request: Return the top ten orders by quantity with order ID, product name, and quantity.

topics.title: GROUP BY
topics.business_skill: Convert transaction rows into business-level summaries.

teaching.teacher:
## GROUP BY
GROUP BY creates one result group per distinct value and allows aggregate functions such as SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, and MAX.
teaching.explain: GROUP BY category with SUM(sales) produces one revenue total per category.
teaching.detailedlearning: Every non-aggregated selected field generally needs to be grouped. Think of GROUP BY as changing the grain from transactions to business groups.
teaching.expose: When the manager asks 'by region', 'by category', or 'per customer', GROUP BY is usually involved.
teaching.example: SELECT category, SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY category;
teaching.business_question: The category manager wants total sales by product category.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT category, SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY category;

questions.request: Return each category and its total sales.
questions.validation: One row per category with SUM(sales).

questions.request: Return each region and total sales.
questions.validation: One row per region with SUM(sales).

questions.scenario: The team is identifying customers with the largest order-book value.
questions.request: Return each customer and total sales generated by that customer.
questions.validation: One row per customer with SUM(sales).

topics.title: HAVING
topics.business_skill: Filter grouped business results using aggregate thresholds.

teaching.teacher:
## HAVING
HAVING filters groups after aggregation. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters grouped results after aggregation.
teaching.explain: HAVING SUM(sales) > 100000 keeps only categories whose total sales exceed the threshold.
teaching.detailedlearning: Use WHERE for row conditions and HAVING for aggregate conditions. This distinction is fundamental to analytical SQL.
teaching.expose: If the condition contains SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, or MAX and applies to groups, think HAVING.
teaching.example: SELECT category, SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY category HAVING SUM(sales) > 100000;
teaching.business_question: The commercial director wants only categories whose total sales exceed 100,000.
teaching.expected_sql: SELECT category, SUM(sales) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY category HAVING SUM(sales) > 100000;

questions.scenario: Management wants only categories generating more than 50,000 in sales.
questions.request: Return category and total sales for qualifying categories.

questions.scenario: The regional manager wants regions with at least 75,000 in sales.
questions.request: Return region and total sales for regions meeting the threshold.

questions.scenario: Leadership wants customers whose cumulative sales exceed 10,000.
questions.request: Return customer name and total sales for customers above the threshold, ordered from highest total sales.
